title: The Three Meanings of Self-Nature
author: Zhanran
excerpt: Question: Many sutras and treatises say that all dharmas are without self-nature. Why does the Lankavatara Sutra say, 'Just as an ox lacks the nature of a horse and a horse lacks the nature of an ox, yet they are not without self-nature'?

inline.s: Question: Many sutras and treatises say that all dharmas are without self-nature. Why does the Lankavatara Sutra say,
“Just as an ox lacks the nature of a horse and a horse lacks the nature of an ox, yet they are not without self-nature”
Answer: The word 'self-nature' has three meanings: first, the essential nature (substance) of a thing, that is, the true marks of all dharmas (for details, see
The True Marks of All Dharmas
); second, the inner spiritual capacity of living beings (for details, see
Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathāgatagarbha
); third, the attributes of things.
[Attribute] A property inherent in a thing itself; a necessary, fundamental, and inseparable characteristic of a thing.

Polysemous words in language satisfy the principle of linguistic economy — using limited vocabulary to reflect the limitless objects of reality — but they also create a certain difficulty for our understanding. Therefore, when reading, one must judge the meaning of such a polysemous word in a given passage according to its context.
The passage of scripture you asked about comes from the Lankavatara Sutra (Mahayana edition):

“Mahāmati! As I have said that all dharmas are without self, it is because there is no selfhood in the dharmas that I say they are without self — it does not mean that all dharmas lack their own self-nature. The meaning of the Tathāgata's words should be understood likewise. Mahāmati! Just as an ox lacks the nature of a horse and a horse lacks the nature of an ox, yet they are not without self-nature.”

Its meaning is: Mahāmati! As I have said that all dharmas are without self, it is because there is no self-essence in the dharmas that I say they are without self (that is, all dharmas are illusions), not that the dharmas lack their respective attributes. The meaning of the words spoken by all Buddhas and Tathāgatas should be understood likewise. Mahāmati! Just as an ox lacks the attributes of a horse and a horse lacks the attributes of an ox, so all dharmas are not without their respective attributes.
In the passage of scripture above, the meaning of 'self-nature' is: the attributes of things.

In this passage, 'all dharmas are without self' is spoken with reference to the true marks of all dharmas, meaning that all dharmas are illusions. Here, 'all dharmas are not without self-nature (all dharmas are not without their respective attributes)' is spoken with reference to the respective attributes of the myriad phenomena in the dream of ignorance. The central idea of this passage is: fundamentally speaking, all dharmas do not exist ('all dharmas are without self'); but with reference to the world of forms in the dream of ignorance, they each have their respective attributes ('all dharmas are not without self-nature'). The former speaks of the essence of the dharmas, and the latter speaks of the marks of the dharmas.

'All dharmas are without self,' in the sutras and treatises is also often expressed as 'all dharmas are without self-nature (all dharmas have no essence of their own),' meaning that all dharmas have no substance and are all illusions, like events in a dream. For example, the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra says:

“For this reason, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, if he grasps at any dharma as existing, as not existing, as both existing and not existing, as neither existing nor not existing, or as not grasping — he is not practicing the prajñāpāramitā. Why is this? Because
(because)
all dharmas are without self-nature and cannot be grasped.”
Here the meaning of 'self-nature' is: the essential nature of a thing
(substance)
, that is, the true marks of all dharmas.
The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“When self-nature is deluded, one is an ordinary being; when self-nature is awakened, one is a Buddha.”
Here the meaning of 'self-nature' is: the inner spiritual capacity of living beings.
